topic: Build your own: state management library

questions.question: Why should the reducer in your store be a pure function `(State, Action) -> State`?
options: Pure functions can be run on the GPU, which makes every state update faster
It lets the store skip copying the state object when each action is handled
Same state and action always give the same result: easy to test and replay
Kotlin only compiles reducers as inline functions when they are free of effects
questions.explanation: Determinism is the whole point: a pure reducer can be unit tested with plain values, and a sequence of actions can be replayed or logged for debugging. Copying still happens, since a new state is returned. Side effects like network calls belong in a separate effects layer.

questions.question: In a Redux-style store, where should a network call triggered by `LoadProfile` run?
options: Inside the reducer, right before it returns the new loading state
In the dispatching composable, launched with `rememberCoroutineScope`
In the State class's init block, so it runs whenever the state is copied
In an effect handler that runs it and dispatches a result action
questions.explanation: The reducer marks the state as loading, and an effect handler does the I/O and later dispatches `ProfileLoaded` or `ProfileFailed`. This keeps the reducer pure and puts async work where it can be cancelled and tested. Calling from the UI ties the request to composition and skips the store's logic.

questions.question: Why does the UI never update after `addItem` is called?
options: StateFlow only emits from the main thread, and `addItem` may run on IO
The same instance is mutated and reassigned, so StateFlow sees no change
A MutableList cannot be used as a property inside a data class
StateFlow needs `emit()` to notify collectors instead of assigning `value`
questions.explanation: StateFlow skips values that are equal to the current one, and here the state object is literally the same instance after the in-place mutation. Use immutable lists and produce a new state with `copy(items = items + x)`. StateFlow's `value` setter is thread-safe and works from any thread.

questions.question: Two coroutines on Dispatchers.Default both run `state.value = state.value.copy(count = state.value.count + 1)` at the same time. Sometimes the count only goes up by one. What is the fix?
options: Use `state.update { it.copy(count = it.count + 1) }`
Mark the `count` property of the state class `@Volatile`
Replace the StateFlow with a SharedFlow that uses replay = 1
Wrap the assignment in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)`
questions.explanation: Reading `value` and then writing it is not atomic, so both coroutines can read the same old count and one increment is lost. `update` does a compare-and-set loop that retries if the value changed in between. Funnelling all actions through one coroutine that processes them in order also works. Volatile and dispatcher changes do not make the read-modify-write atomic.

questions.question: With Compose strong skipping enabled, a composable takes `items: List<Item>`. Its parent recomposes and passes a new List with the same contents. Does the child skip?
options: Yes, because List parameters are always compared with equals() before skipping
No, because composables that take List parameters can never skip at all
Yes, because strong skipping skips any composable whose parameter types match
No: unstable parameters are compared by identity, and this is a new instance
questions.explanation: Strong skipping lets composables with unstable parameters skip, but compares those parameters with `===`, while stable ones use `equals()`. A new List instance therefore triggers recomposition even if it is equal. Keeping the same instance when nothing changed, or using an immutable collection type the compiler treats as stable, restores skipping.

questions.question: Which of these can cause a one-off event such as "show snackbar" to be lost or shown twice? Select all that apply.
options: Emitting it on a SharedFlow with replay = 0 while no collector is active
Keeping the reducer pure and returning the event as part of the new state
Keeping it in state and having the UI report back once it has been shown, which clears it
Holding it in a StateFlow field that is never cleared, so it shows again after rotation
questions.explanation: A SharedFlow without replay drops values when nobody is collecting, for example during a configuration change. A StateFlow field that is never consumed is redelivered to every new collector. Modelling the event as state that the UI acknowledges is the pattern designed to avoid both problems.

questions.question: Each keystroke dispatches `Search(query)`, and its effect starts a network request. Results for old queries sometimes arrive last and overwrite the newest ones. What should the library provide?
options: A bigger thread pool for effects so every request finishes sooner
A reducer rule that drops any result older than one second
Keyed effects: a new effect with the same key cancels the old one
A debounce inside the reducer so only every third keystroke is handled
questions.explanation: Cancelling the previous effect for the same key, like `flatMapLatest` or `collectLatest`, guarantees only the latest query's result is applied. Debouncing reduces calls but does not stop an older response from arriving last. Timing heuristics in the reducer make it impure and are still racy.

questions.question: The lambda passed to `MutableStateFlow.update { }` may run more than once for a single call, so it must not have side effects.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. `update` reads the value, runs the lambda, and does a compare-and-set; if another writer got in first, it runs the lambda again with the new value. Logging an analytics event or launching a job inside it can therefore happen multiple times.

questions.question: A reducer may launch a coroutine to fetch data, as long as it still returns the new state synchronously.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Launching work from the reducer makes it impure, untestable as a plain function, and hard to cancel. The reducer should only compute the next state; an effect layer runs the fetch and dispatches its result.

questions.question: Your store must restore well after process death. Which are good design choices? Select all that apply.
options: Persist only the minimal input state, such as IDs and form fields, through SavedStateHandle
Keep the store in a top-level singleton so it survives process death
Serialize the entire state, including large lists, into the saved state Bundle
Re-fetch remote or derived data after restore instead of saving it
questions.explanation: Saved state is size-limited, so store what the user cannot recover (what they typed, what they selected) and reload the rest. Large lists risk TransactionTooLargeException. A singleton lives in process memory, so it dies with the process like everything else.
